Neuromorphic Photonic Circuits Using Post-Fabrication

Lei Xu,* Jiawei Zhang, Eli A. Doris, Simon Bilodeau, Jesse A. Wisch, Manting Gui,
Yusuf O. Jimoh, Bhavin Shastri, Barry P. Rand,* and Paul R. Prucnal*
Neuromorphic photonics has become one of the research forefronts in
photonics, with its beneﬁts in low-latency signal processing and potential
in signiﬁcant energy consumption reduction when compared with digital
electronics. With artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) computing accelerators in high
demand, one of the high-impact research goals is to build scalable neuro-
morphic photonic integrated circuits which can accelerate the computing
of AI models at high energy eﬃciency. A complete neuromorphic photonic
computing system comprises seven stacks: materials, devices, circuits,
microarchitecture, system architecture, algorithms, and applications. Here, we
consider microring resonator (MRR)-based network designs toward building
scalable silicon integrated photonic neural networks (PNN), and variations
of MRR resonance wavelength from the fabrication process and their
impact on PNN scalability. Further, post-fabrication processing using organic
photochromic layers over the silicon platform is shown to be eﬀective for
trimming MRR resonance wavelength variation, which can signiﬁcantly reduce
energy consumption from the MRR-based PNN conﬁguration. Post-fabrication
processing with photochromic materials to compensate for the variation in
MRR fabrication will allow a scalable silicon system on a chip without sacriﬁcing
today’s performance metrics, which will be critical for the commercial
viability and volume production of large-scale silicon photonic circuits.

1. Introduction
Silicon photonic integrated circuits have
made enormous progress recently, ranging
from commercial success in high-volume
production of optical transceivers for data
centers to advances in silicon neuromor-
phic photonic computing and photonic ma-
trix multiplication networks.[1,2] The fabri-
cation of silicon photonic chips leverages
the capabilities and services of foundries
to build integrated waveguides and pho-
tonic devices to process light wave signals at
various wavelengths.[1] Based on diﬀerent
operating principles from electronic chips,
silicon photonic chips have the potential
to disrupt the current artiﬁcial intelligence
(AI)-driven computing paradigm, promis-
ing multiple orders of magnitude improve-
ments to computing speed, latency and
energy consumption.[2] With participation
of leading foundries in supporting silicon
photonic chip runs and business model in-
novations, such as multi-project wafer runs,
it has become easily accessible for academic
research groups to design and fabricate sil-
icon photonic chips, even at scales that
accomodate a large number of photonic components. The recent
trend in AI computing is the large language models,[3] which
are implemented through large-scale parallel processing of high-
volume datasets. To the silicon photonics research community,
the trend has posed a real challenge, which is to develop tech-
nologies toward building scalable photonic computing systems.
Following a typical neuromorphic computing system hierar-
chy in ref. [4], a neuromorphic photonic computing system in-
cluding hardware and software has a hierarchical division of
seven layers or stacks: materials, devices, circuits, microarchi-
tecture, system architecture, algorithm and applications. On the
one hand, co-design across the seven compute stacks enables al-
gorithms and applications to inﬂuence the underlying hardware
design,[4] and on the other hand, bottom stacks such as materials
and devices can directly impact the other compute stacks as well
as the overall system performance.
Along with the fact that silicon photonic devices typically have
much larger footprints than integrated electronic transistors, an-
other limitation of silicon photonic integrated circuits is the
photonic device performance variations from the micro/nano

the same set of MRR design parameters can result in nanometer-

using MRR-based weight banks, each MRR is expected to be

processing using organic photochromic thin ﬁlms deposited on a
silicon photonic platform and trimming the transmission charac-

ogy can eliminate the unwanted MRR transmission variations,
and enable further research on building MRR-based PNN chips
at scale.
The principle of scalable neuromorphic photonic systems are
presented in section 2; MRR post-fabrication errors are discussed
in Section 3. Section 4 presents recent work on photochromic
materials in silicon photonic platforms and trimming the trans-
mission characteristics of MRRs. In Section 5, future research
on leveraging maskless laser writing over photochromic thin
ﬁlms on silicon photonic platforms for trimming photonic de-
vices is discussed.
2. Neuromorphic Photonics
Neuromorphic photonics, involving building interconnected
photonic neurons to support signal processing and computing
applications, has made signiﬁcant progress and attracted consid-
erable attention recently.[2] Figure 1a,b shows the biological neu-
ron and a model of how signals are processed within a single
neuron, respectively. Each neuron is responsible for receiving,
processing and transmitting information with other connected
neurons. In a biological neuron, electrical or electrochemical sig-
nals are received through dendrites, and impulses or spiking
signals are generated by the neuron and carried away by axon
for interconnection with other neurons through axon terminals,
as shown in Figure 1a. The spiking signal is generated follow-
ing three key steps of weighting to each input, summation, and
nonlinear operation to the sum. Communication and informa-
tion processing through a large number of interconnected neu-
rons in a human brain enable our intelligence and complex daily
functionalities.
With a small number of nodes, neuromorphic photonic
chips have demonstrated applications in processing time series
data, including ﬁber nonlinearity compensation for transoceanic
communication,[10]
and wireless signal processing,[11]
and
achieving ultra-low latency and broadband signal processing. To-
ward AI computing, PNN chips can potentially achieve signiﬁ-
cant energy eﬃciency improvements.[9,12]
From a materials perspective, early research on PNNs has
demonstrated a free-space optical system for optical implemen-
tation of the Hopﬁeld model,[14,15] an optical ﬁber and III-V semi-
conductor optical ampliﬁer (SOA) system to show correspon-
dence between the electrical model of leaky integration of mem-
brane voltage and optical models,[16] a III-V platform to achieve
photodetector-driving excitable lasers or spiking lasers,[17] and
a silicon photonic platform to ﬁrst show MRR-based weight
banks.[18] A comprehensive review of photonics for artiﬁcial in-
telligence and neuromorphic computing can be found in ref. [2].

2.1. Photonic Neural Networks with Wavelength Division
Multiplexing
Figure 1c shows a typical feedforward PNN, and each of the
nodes can be implemented using integrated photonic circuits
shown in Figure 1d. The PNN has a large number of iden-
tical photonic nodes which are interconnected using a set
of standard wavelengths on International-Telecommunication-
Union (ITU) grids,[19] known as wavelength division multiplex-
ing (WDM). Each of the wavelength-carrying data channel is pre-
cisely weighted by MRRs, as shown in Figure 1d. Each set of
MRRs form a microring weight bank (w1, w2, w3, …, wN), which
can simultaneously weight N wavelength (carrying data) chan-
nels. For a PNN with p nodes and n wavelengths, there are p ×
n MRRs, among which p of them operating on the same wave-
length should have exactly the same functional parameters. Fol-
lowing the guidelines on ITU grids, there are 40, 80, or 160 stan-
dard wavelengths available on 100 GHz, 50 GHz or 25 GHz chan-
nel spacing, respectively. The weighting, summation, and non-
linear transformation in Figure 1b can be mapped into the MRR-
based integrated photonic circuits shown in Figure 1d.
Weighting: In a multi-wavelength or WDM photonic neuron,
the multiple input signals (x1, x2, …, xN) are encoded over diﬀer-
ent wavelengths (𝜆1, 𝜆2, …, 𝜆N,) to form optical channels (x1(𝜆1),
x2(𝜆2), …, xN(𝜆N)). Each channel represents the input signal from
other photonic neurons. These WDM signals are combined to a
common output waveguide typically via a WDM multiplexer. The
WDM multiplexer has a ﬁxed insertion loss in comparison with
a simpler optical coupler whose insertion loss increases with a
larger number of channels. The combined WDM signals within
the same waveguide pass through microring weight banks as
shown in Figure 1d. Each of the MRRs is designed to match
its resonance wavelength with one of the input wavelengths and
control its weighting independently by adjusting the resonance
to change the transmission coeﬃcient on the input wavelength.
And MRRs with precise weighting can be implemented with
in-ring photoconductive heaters with N doping.[10,20–22] Contin-
uously, multi-channel control with accuracy over 8 bits has been
demonstrated,[8] which is comparable to the resolution of matrix
multipliers used in digital signal processing application speciﬁc
integrated circuits (ASICs).
Summation: The weighted optical signals after the parallel
weighting of an array of MRRs at diﬀerent wavelengths (weight
banks) are split into the through and drop ports of MRR, and
the splitting ratio of each wavelength is decided by the weight-
ing of the corresponding MRR. The two output ports are optical-
to-electrical converted by balanced germanium-on-silicon pho-
todetectors (BPDs) with subtraction,[23] and the BPDs linearly
transform the sum of the optical signals to photocurrent. From a
system design perspective, the signal bandwidth on each of the
WDM channels should be less than half the WDM channel spac-
ing to avoid beating noise after photodetection (a typical WDM
system has equal channel spacing for 𝜆1, 𝜆2, …, 𝜆N).
Nonlinear Transformation: There have been two types of pho-
tonic neurons: non-spiking and spiking. The photocurrent after
BPD is sent to a silicon MRR modulator (MRM)[24] as input to
a non-spiking neuron shown in Figure 1d, or to drive a two-
section excitable laser[17] for a spiking photonic neuron. A non-
spiking neuron can leverage the silicon photonics platform and
foundry fabrication by integrating the weight bank, BPDs, and
MRMs on the same chip in scale, and oﬀ-chip laser sources or
WDM laser arrays can be coupled to the silicon photonic chip. In
order to take advantage of silicon photonics fabrication, a spik-
ing PNN can be developed using both silicon photonics for mi-
croring weight banks and BPDs, and group III–V semiconduc-
tors for optical gain and lasers, with heterogeneous co-integration
technologies.[25] In the non-spiking photonic neuron shown in
Figure 1d, the combined photocurrents generated by the BPD
drive the microring modulator via free-carrier injection to the p-
n junction. An oﬀ-chip light source (pump laser at wavelength 𝜆k)
is sent to the optical input port of the MRM, and the optical out-
put will carry the nonlinearity 𝜑deﬁned by the MRM’s electrical-
to-optical transfer function largely caused by the carrier-induced
nonlinearity. The nonlinear transfer function has been demon-
strated to be programmable by adjusting the bias currents to the
p-n junction of a MRM.[24]
When compared with an electrical computing processor, a
neuromorphic photonic computing processor brings distinctive
beneﬁts. Some of them are:
a) Analog optical circuits process broadband signals in their na-
tive format. Instead of following digital clock speeds, an ana-
log photonic system can process signals in time-of-ﬂight. For
example, in a silicon waveguide, it takes optical signals at 1550
nm 12 ps to travel 1 mm. Sub-picosecond signal processing
can be achieved with photonic integrated circuits having total
optical path less than 1 mm.[26]
b) WDM provides scalable interconnections and routing. Con-
sidering the commercially available WDM channel counts
(40-160 channels in C band at standard channel spacing) and

2.2. Scalable Photonic Neural Networks
Silicon photonics leverages foundries which have sophisticated
and reliable semiconductor device processing, to produce pho-
tonic integrated circuits with high yield rate and robustness.[1] In
comparison with free-space or ﬁber components-based photonic
systems, silicon photonic integrated circuits can enable signiﬁ-
cant reduction in size, weight, and cost, all of which are desir-
able features for commercialization. For example, silicon pho-
tonics has been shown to be well-suited for high-speed digital
coherent optical communications, and has driven the develop-
ment and deployment of high-speed pluggable transceivers for
data centers.[28]
Silicon photonics has demonstrated success in MRR-based
neuromorphic photonic chip design and fabrication, and enabled
applications to achieve performance beyond what electronics can
attain, with only a small number of photonic neurons.[10,29,30]
With the recent development of large language models for ma-
chine learning and AI, large scale PNNs which can operate with
low latency and high energy eﬃciency are of very high impact for
the future of AI hardware. From a foundry perspective, silicon
photonic integrated circuits can reach very high device densities
and wafer-scale photonic chips can potentially have a very large
number of photonic devices (device dimension varies from 10s to
100s of microns). Following the MRR-based photonic neuron de-
sign shown in Figure 1(d), we review some of the key PNN archi-
tectures and discuss their applications in diﬀerent scales, from a
single chip, inter-chip on the same circuit board (intra-board), to
intra-rack and intra-data center systems.

within the same broadcast-and-weight loop. Some of the speciﬁc
design considerations include: 1) the upper limit of the number

2.3. Neuromorphic Photonic System Stacks
Building a functional neuromorphic photonic system requires
us to look into the seven-stack hierarchy shown in Figure 4[4]:
ﬁve (5) hardware stacks (materials, devices, circuits, microarchi-
tecture, system architecture), and two (2) software stacks (algo-
rithms and applications). In the current state-of-the-art electronic
computing systems (such as personal computers or server racks),
the seven stacks follow a bottom-up approach, in which the lower
stack informs the immediate upper stack sequentially, as shown
in Figure 4a.[4] The upper software stacks use the hardware ab-
straction to design and optimize applications.
Now, with the designs and implementation of photonic neu-
rons using WDM and silicon photonics together with the scal-
able system architecture in Section 2.2, the question is whether
it is ready to build a functional large-scale neuromorphic pho-
tonic computing system within a single chip or across multi-
ple chips, which can run and test machine learning/AI com-
puting models with a large number of parameters. The map-
ping of state-of-the-art progress in both hardware and software
aspects of silicon neuromorphic photonic computing shows a hi-
erarchical division with similar seven layers of abstraction, as
shown in Figure 4b. In comparison with the electronic com-
puting hierarchy, the seven stacks in neuromorphic comput-

3. MRR Resonance Wavelength Variations From
Fabrication
In Figure 2, there are 16 MRRs for weighting and four MRRs

6. Conclusions
Despite the available capability of foundries to fabricate photonic
chips at scale, most demonstrated neuromorphic photonic chips
are at very small scale in terms of having a single digit number
of photonic neurons. Toward building a multi-functional, large-
scale neuromorphic photonic system, each of the seven comput-
ing stacks needs to be comprehensively addressed. In this paper,
we show a neuromorphic photonic system architecture which is
suitable for single-chip, inter-chip, intra-rack, and intra-data cen-
ter scale applications. On the material and device layers, we target
to solve the MRR fabrication variations through trimming using
photochromic thin ﬁlms on a silicon photonic circuits platform.
We envision that a new silicon photonic chip manufacturing pro-
cess with foundry fabrication followed by photochromic material
deposition and maskless laser writing can potentially produce
photonic chips with predictable performance and reduce the en-
ergy consumption from thermal tuning, which will further clear
the way for large-scale silicon photonic chip manufacturing and
commercialization for applications in sensing, communication,
and computing.
